cues.text: Let's turn now to incident response and disclosure ethics.
When something goes wrong with a system that holds data, what do we do, in what order, and what do we owe to the people affected?
This chapter answers those questions.
Start with the incident lifecycle.
It has six stages, and the order matters.
First, preparation.
Second, detection and analysis.
Third, containment.
Fourth, eradication.
Fifth, recovery.
And sixth, lessons learned.
Preparation happens before anything goes wrong: the plans, the roles and the tools.
Detection and analysis is where you discover that something has happened and work out what it actually is.
Containment limits the spread.
Eradication removes the cause.
Recovery restores normal operations.
Lessons learned closes the loop, and we will return to it at the end.
Alongside these stages, the source sets out several working duties.
Preserve evidence and maintain chain of custody.
Chain of custody means being able to show who handled the evidence, when, and what they did with it, so that it can be trusted later.
Record your actions and their timestamps.
Contain the incident without destroying important evidence.
That is a real tension.
The urge to wipe a machine and move on can destroy exactly what investigators need.
And finally, notify clients, regulators and affected individuals as required, based on the actual facts and scope of the incident.
Notice the phrase "actual facts and scope".
Notification should follow what you have established, not guesswork in either direction.
Now to the legal timing rules, where precision is essential.
Under the NDPA, the Nigeria Data Protection Act, a processor reports to the relevant controller, or to the relevant processor, upon becoming aware of a breach.
The controller then assesses the statutory risk threshold and applies the 72-hour rule for notifying the NDPC, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission.
That 72 hours runs from awareness.
Under the GDPR, the General Data Protection Regulation, notification to the supervisory authority is required within 72 hours where feasible, unless the breach is unlikely to result in risk.
Separately, where individuals face high risk, there are distinct duties towards those individuals themselves.
HIPAA, the United States health privacy framework, is different.
Its rules concern qualifying breaches of unsecured PHI, that is, protected health information, and it generally has different deadlines.
The source gives a clear warning: do not impose a universal 72-hour rule across all frameworks.
The NDPA and the GDPR share a 72-hour figure, but each has its own conditions, and HIPAA works differently.
Always ask which framework applies before quoting a deadline.
Now the ethical dimension.
Ethically, delay or concealment can increase harm and undermine autonomy, even when the exact legal duty is uncertain.
Autonomy here means people's ability to protect themselves, for example by changing passwords or watching their accounts, which they cannot do if they have not been told.
So what should good communication contain?
Known facts.
Unknowns, stated honestly.
Protective actions people can take.
Contact points.
And when the next update will come.
Two cautions follow.
Avoid prematurely claiming there was no compromise, because you may have to retract it.
And avoid publishing sensitive investigation detail that could help attackers or harm the inquiry.
The source also says to coordinate legal, technical and management decisions in parallel, not one after another, so that none of them stalls the others.
Then comes a key distinction.
Legal obligations and moral responsibilities overlap, but they are not identical.
The source's example: a vulnerability may warrant client notification even before evidence confirms a personal-data breach.
The law may not yet require it, but responsibility to the people who depend on you may still point toward telling them.
Finally, lessons learned.
After recovery, conduct a root-cause review.
Assign corrective actions.
Improve policy and training.
Reassess vendors and controls.
And verify that the mitigations actually operate, because a fix on paper is not a fix.
Throughout, distinguish individual mistakes from systemic incentives, resource gaps and management failures.
A single person's error is often the visible tip of a deeper problem, such as pressure to ship quickly or too little budget for security.
And the source ends on this point: a blame-only culture discourages early reporting.
If people fear punishment, they hide problems, and early reporting is exactly what shortens an incident and reduces harm.
